title: Punjab's drug crisis
hookLine: families and gurdwaras are working to help young people out of addiction

lines: A MOTHER HOLDS HER SON'S PHONE.
cards: A mother sits on the steps outside a gurdwara, holding her son's phone. He asked her to keep it. He's a few days into trying to stop, and he doesn't trust himself with the numbers saved inside.
Through the doors, kirtan is playing. A volunteer brings her a cup of tea and sits down beside her without asking a single question.
In Punjab, families have been living stories like this, and talking about them at kitchen tables, in songs and in the gurdwara. Today isn't about blame. It's about the hands reaching in.

teach.b: Addiction in Punjab has reached into homes: a son, a cousin, a classmate, a neighbor's boy who used to play cricket in the lane. There are figures, and people argue about them.
This lesson leaves them out, because behind every one is a person with a name.

At Ang 554 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Amar Das describes what the false wine does: drinking it, a person loses their sense, can't tell their own from a stranger, and is pushed away from the Master.

teach.h: ANG 554: DON'T DRINK THE FALSE WINE.
teach.b: So, he says, don't drink this false wine at all, if it is in your power.

The Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, carries the same teaching: it asks Sikhs to keep away from intoxicants, and names liquor, tobacco, opium and hemp among them. But the salok doesn't stop at the warning.

teach.h: A TRUE WINE, FOUND BY GRACE.
teach.b: It speaks of a true wine, found by grace, by the one who meets the True Guru. It doesn't only take something away; it points to something to fill the empty place. Then the hands.
Families, doctors and sangats work on this together. Some gurdwaras and Sikh groups support recovery programs, sports for young people and kirtan classes.
Some sangats have learned to sit with a family instead of whispering about it. Shame keeps people hidden. A sangat that pulls up a chair makes it easier to come out.
Not lecture them out. Not shame them out.

how: The Sikh Rehat Maryada asks Sikhs to avoid intoxicants. Some gurdwaras and Sikh organizations in Punjab and abroad support recovery work, youth programs and families facing addiction, alongside medical treatment.

o: intoxication, the false wine that clouds the mind
a strong craving for something sweet to eat
a heavy, sleepy calm after a big meal

games.q: the warning and the help — tap the pairs.
p: found by grace, meeting the True Guru
sits with the family, no whispers

s: the salok at Ang 554 only warns and stops there
it also speaks of a true wine, found by grace, by the one who meets the True Guru.
the Sikh code of conduct asks Sikhs to keep away from intoxicants
the Rehat Maryada names liquor, tobacco, opium and hemp among them.
helping someone out means lecturing them
today's story is tea with no questions, recovery programs and a sangat that sits with the family.

games.q: a young man in your sangat is using, and his family has stopped coming to the gurdwara out of shame. what does today's story point to?
o: leave them alone; it's a private shame.
sit with the family and help him toward care.
ask him to stay away until he's better.
games.why: families and gurdwaras are working to help young people out. shame keeps people hidden; a chair pulled up to the table makes it easier to come out.

practice: Go back to the gurdwara steps and take the volunteer's place: a cup of tea in your hands, beside someone carrying something heavy, maybe the mother, maybe someone you know who is struggling with a drink, a drug, a screen, grief, or something they haven't told anyone.
Don't speak and don't fix anything; feel the warmth of the cup and keep your place on the step, because sitting there is the whole job. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Nasha. Intoxication, the addiction that has reached into Punjabi homes, with families, gurdwaras and doctors working to bring young people out of it. Today's word.

orig.note: nasha, the Punjabi word for intoxication.

carryVoice: Your line: help them out. And if someone is in danger, get them to a doctor or emergency help first. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Ang 554 (Bihagra ki Var, salok of Guru Amar Das on the false wine and the true wine)
